Tirupati: Municipal Corporation Commissioner M Jayakrishna has directed officials to conduct the corporation’s general elections with utmost care, transparency and impartiality, strictly following the election code and all related rules.
Addressing Returning Officers and Assistant Returning.
Officers at a meeting here on Wednesday, the Commissioner said election code came into force and must be observed from filing of nominations until completion of the election process.
He instructed all officials to avoid errors and discharge their duties in accordance with the State Election Commission’s guidelines.
Jayakrishna asked officials at nomination reception centres to remain alert and handle the nomination process carefully, while directing Presiding.
Officers to read the relevant rulebooks thoroughly and ensure that no mistakes occur during nominations.
He also stressed the need for close coordination among officials at every stage of the election.
Additional Commissioner Sarada Devi, Deputy Commissioner Amaraiah, Bharat Naik, SE Syam Sundar and Tahsildar Suresh Babu attended the meeting.

stories.headline: Houthi missile hits Aramco building in Saudi Arabia, four injured in Riyadh
stories.title: Houthi missile hits Aramco building in Saudi Arabia, four injured in Riyadh
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 14: A missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi movement struck a building belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran overnight, escalating the confrontation between the Iran-backed group and the Saudi-led coalition, the BBC reported. Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said the attack caused a “limited fire” in an administrative building at Aramco’s headquarters. Saudi authorities also reported that several missiles and drones were intercepted elsewhere, while falling debris injured four people in the capital, Riyadh. The attack came after the Saudi-led coalition struck a fuel depot operated by the Yemen Petroleum Company at al-Sabaha, near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, on Tuesday. The Houthis said they had targeted Aramco and Riyadh’s airport in retaliation for the coalition’s strike and warned that further attacks would follow in the coming days. The latest escalation has further heightened concerns over the security of Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure and the potential disruption of regional oil supplies and international shipping. BBC reported that International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that the intensifying conflict could have “potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere”. The Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, had vowed on Tuesday that the Houthis would “bear the consequences” of their recent attacks on the kingdom. The warning followed a missile strike on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday that killed 13 people including an Indian. The Houthis have also claimed responsibility for attacks targeting Saudi airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases. The group has said its attacks are retaliation for Saudi air strikes on areas under its control in western Yemen, including Sanaa. The renewed confrontation comes amid escalating fighting along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and serves as a key gateway to the Suez Canal. The growing threat to energy facilities and shipping routes has raised concerns over wider regional instability and its implications for global trade. Yemen has been engulfed in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition intervened in support of the internationally recognised government.

stories.headline: NC manifesto hangs in balance as CM Omar-led govt completes 2 years in office tomorrow
stories.title: NC manifesto hangs in balance as CM Omar-led govt completes 2 years in office tomorrow
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 14: They say – there’s many a slip between the cup and the lip! “Red letter day” of October 16 is just round the corner- precisely just a day away – when the incumbent elected government, led by the Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, will complete its second year in office in the Union Territory set-up of Jammu and Kashmir. So here comes the perfect appraisal time to count those slips between the “cup” and the “lip”, though not in proverbial dimensions. In the context of appraisal, “lip” will denote promises by the helmsmen and “cup” – their delivery to “the ruled”. It’s time to measure and judge to what extent “Dignity, Identity and Development” promised as a “solemn pledge” to the people reached their doorsteps. If one goes by the shriller voices in the corridors of power, statehood has remained the dominant chorus – the fulcrum of the ruling alliance of National Conference-Congress’ political juggernaut throughout the year. The plank continued to offer as an impenetrable shield to the alliance and particularly the National Conference against the opposition’s unrelenting onslaught. Unlike his reconciliatory approach during the first year in office, second year saw CM Omar stridently fighting, protesting for restoration of statehood and projecting that its (statehood’s) absence only caused all the “slips” between the “cup” and the “lip” to blunt opposition’s offensive vis-à-vis non fulfilment of poll promises (by NC). Interestingly, the government, fully aware of harsh realities of politics, during its second year in power, has less relied on its trite plank during first one year that its mandate to fulfil poll promises is for five years and not one, two or three years - to duck prickly queries of both the opposition and the people. As a sagacious old player in the political arena, it has focussed more on “absence of statehood” to shift the burden of its “complete failure in governance”, (as alleged by its detractors), on its political opponents (read BJP only) as well. But does it convince the opposition, which has already written off the NC-led alliance government as “Failed” consecutively in its second Annual Performance Report (APR) or the people – the ruled? Absolutely not – in case of opposition! In the case of people, nothing can be said with certainty as they actually speak only after five years through votes! To be fair, it (NC government) has tried to take baby- steps towards the realisation of several of its promises made in its manifesto. Though it’s a story for another day that most of those steps, so far, have proved to be nothing more than paper-horses – the distance between the cup and the lip persists. Keeping the “paper-horses” proposition in mind, one can tick mark the boxes while sifting through its 12 guarantees, as mentioned in NC manifesto 2024. With regard to its first guarantee related to “Restoration of political and legal status” – it continues to strive for “full implementation of autonomy resolution”; “restoration of Articles 370 and 35 A” and statehood as prior to August 5, 2019. The government has kept its promise – it is striving for all three “big guarantees.” But how will it continue to strive for them? None has any idea and even the government, itself, is clueless. In any case, except statehood, two other guarantees can justifiably be not part of the government's real APR (other than the wordy duel). However, it kept its word to move resolutions in the assembly and get them passed. While it succeeded in reviving its autonomy resolution of 2000 in the just concluded autumn session of J&K Legislature, the words Articles 370 and 35-A could not see their verbatim entry in any of resolutions passed so far by the House or the J&K Council of Ministers. Cornered by the opposition in this context, the government maintained that the word “special status” mentioned in the resolutions was their (Articles 370 n 35-A’s) cloak. It had promised to make endeavours to redraw the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 and the transaction of Business of the Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir Rules, 2019. As promised, its endeavours continued even when it’s about to complete its second year in office. “Files remained pending with the Centre,” the government reaffirms. The status of files related to tweaking of reservation rules (policy), committee report about regularisation of daily wagers too remains in knowledge of government only. Opaqueness persists about the efforts to “modify, annul and repeal post August 5, 2019 laws impacting J&K’s special status”; “protect the land and employment rights of the people of J&K” and “secure the release of prisoners languishing in jails.” But as they are some tricky propositions, it will be fair enough to push their APR to 2029. Similar is the status about the guarantee to repeal the Public Safety Act (PSA). One can wait for these guarantees to fructify, even after 2029. But the opposition and people can genuinely question the status of guarantee to “fill up all vacancies in government departments within 180 days” and realisation of other related promises on the ground (beyond announcement and flurry of paper horses). Next guarantee related to “200 units of electricity free”. In the manifesto, there were no strings attached to it. But in the current scenario, as opposition, too, repeatedly targets – the government has shifted its “goal post to AAY families” and now it is linked to “PM Surya GharMuftBijliYojana” of Government of India. Moving on, does anyone remember that the party has given a guarantee to “provide Rs 5000 per month to female heads of EWS households”? If not, forget it. EWS (families) to get 12 cylinders free of cost per year - was another guarantee. The government, in its second year, endeavoured to fulfil this promise partially and with “strings attached.” It has kept its promises to enhance the old age and widow pension, free ride for women (with partial tweaking) in e-buses and free education (for all) with a tweaked proposition. It has been successful in restoration of Darbar Move in its second year. The government has maintained that it has also fulfilled its poll promise related to “Ease of Doing Business” with the passage of a related bill in the just concluded autumn session. Rest of its major guarantees and promises remain out of its own realm so far and this gives the opposition a handle to beat it, in an unrelenting manner. “How dual power is creating obstruction in good governance? On statehood, earlier NC (other parties’) stance was - it would come on its own and we will have to wage a bigger war for Art 370 and 35 A. Youth continue to be incarcerated in jails outside J&K. What has happened to 12 free cylinders to all? There were certain achievable goals even within the UT setup, they (NC government) could not get them even,” maintains former minister and senior leader of J&K Apni Party, G H Mir, while talking to GKTV. He claimed that in 1983, NC in its manifesto had promised to ensure posts for Chief Secretary, DGP and Chief Justice for J&K citizens but after coming to power, it brought Chief Secretary from outside. “When there was statehood, they wanted autonomy. In the current scenario, they are seeking statehood. It simply means they don’t want to deliver. We too support statehood demand. But their (NC’s) politics always revolves around exploitation of people’s sentiments by provoking them against the Centre and not good governance. They are now resorting to confrontational politics. Confrontation is not going to help it, anyway. It did not help in the past, it will not help even now,” Mir points out. “The election happened under the UT setup to govern a Union Territory. The Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, himself, was on record saying that he had served as the Chief Minister of State so it would be embarrassing for him to contest for power in UT. But he did and won power. However, he could not effectively use powers even within the UT set up to make people’s life better. Dual power is a system prevalent at many places but it cannot be used as an excuse to deprive the people of good governance or one promised to them (people) while contesting for UT. How is the dual system obstructing filling of vacant posts,” former minister argues. Leader of the Opposition in J&K Legislature Sunil Sharma too has repeatedly targeted the government for using “statehood” as a plank to “cover-up its failure to fulfil poll promises.” “Corruption has become deeply entrenched under the present dispensation, while transparency and accountability have been completely sidelined. The government's policy of outsourcing jobs without establishing a transparent and foolproof recruitment mechanism,” he alleges, adding, “Such policies created ample space for manipulation, favouritism and corruption while depriving deserving youth of fair employment opportunities.” J&K BJP leadership also criticises NC government, for what it alleges, “deliberately resorting to dirty tactics to delay Panchayat elections, weaken the Panchayati Raj Institutions and obstruct the functioning of the three-tier democratic system in Jammu and Kashmir.” “The grassroots democracy could not be sacrificed for political convenience,” BJP leaders assert.

stories.headline: Ajay Devgn returns to Kargil after 23 years for ‘Chauhaan’ shoot
stories.title: Ajay Devgn returns to Kargil after 23 years for ‘Chauhaan’ shoot
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 14: Bollywood actor Ajay Devgn has returned to Kargil in Ladakh after a gap of 23 years to shoot his upcoming film Chauhaan, bringing him back to the mountainous region where he earlier filmed portions of the 2003 war drama LOC: Kargil. Devgn has begun filming the action drama in Kargil, with reports indicating that several important sequences will be shot in the region. A member of the production team overseeing the shoot told Rising Kashmir that the actor had arrived in Kargil and filming had begun. “The actor will shoot at different locations across Kargil, and the schedule is expected to conclude on October 26,” he said. The film is directed by Neeraj Yadav and produced by Jyoti Deshpande, Aanand L Rai and Himanshu Sharma under Jio Studios and Colour Yellow Productions. The film is scheduled for theatrical release on October 1, 2027. The project was announced on June 25, 2026, the birth anniversary of Devgn’s late father, action director Veeru Devgan. Its promotional video introduced the actor in an intense action avatar and ended with the dialogue, “Pathaanon se kehna, Chauhaan aa raha hai” (Tell the Pathaans, Chauhaan is coming). Rising Kashmir has learnt that the actor is enjoying Kargil’s cold weather, much like he did during an earlier shoot in the region in 2003. Devgn’s association with Jammu and Kashmir extends beyond his two visits to Ladakh for LOC: Kargil and Chauhaan. In 1999, he starred in Dil Kya Kare, directed by Prakash Jha and produced by his father, Veeru Devgan, alongside Veena Devgan and Kumaar Mangat. The film featured Kajol, Mahima Chaudhry and Chandrachur Singh and explored themes of love, family and difficult personal choices. In 2024, Devgn returned to Kashmir for Rohit Shetty’s Singham Again, the fifth instalment in the filmmaker’s popular cop universe. The film’s shooting schedule included sequences filmed in Srinagar’s downtown, Lal Chowk and Sonamarg in May 2024, with Devgn appearing alongside Jackie Shroff. The shoot drew attention from residents as the production team filmed action sequences under tight security.

stories.headline: Kashmirification of Delhi
stories.title: Kashmirification of Delhi
stories.summary: There is something profoundly revealing about the images emerging from New Delhi ahead of the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar. Barricaded roads, restrictions on movement, suspended internet services, cancelled trains, detained students and a massive deployment of security personnel. A national capital preparing to contain its own citizens raises a question that should trouble every believer in constitutional democracy: why does a government that derives its authority from the people appear so apprehensive when those very people assemble to question it? For Kashmiris, this spectacle is not unfamiliar. It is a reminder of August 2019, when Jammu and Kashmir was placed under sweeping restrictions, communication networks were shut down and political life was profoundly disrupted as the Union Government proceeded to abrogate Article 370 and reorganise the state. What Delhi is reportedly experiencing today, Kashmir has known for years. The difference is that Kashmiris were expected to accept it as normal. What happened to Kashmir in 2019? On 5 August 2019, the constitutional changes relating to Article 370 were announced. Parliament subsequently passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which came into effect on 31 October 2019. The former state was divided into two Union Territories, Jammu and Kashmir with a legislature and Ladakh without one. Consider the magnitude of this transformation. A full fledged state, with its own elected legislature and constitutional arrangements, ceased to exist in its previous form. Its political status was fundamentally altered. The suspension of ordinary freedoms, the containment of dissent and the expansion of executive control can create a democratic crisis even when constitutional institutions continue to function. Elections alone cannot settle the question. A government may win an electoral mandate and still be required to justify its restrictions, answer criticism and respect the rights of its opponents. The purpose of democracy is not to make governments comfortable. It is to make power accountable. The test of India’s democracy Kashmir has never asked for its people to be treated as an exception to India’s constitutional promises. It has asked that those promises be honoured. It has asked that its political future not be treated as a matter exclusively for distant authorities. It has asked for statehood, accountable government and the dignity of meaningful democratic participation. If the rest of India is now confronting questions that Kashmir has raised for years, will it finally listen? Will the national conversation recognise that the rights of Kashmiris were never merely a regional concern? Will institutions insist that restrictions on peaceful assembly and communication be justified under the Constitution, regardless of where they occur? Will the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood be treated as a serious democratic commitment rather than an indefinitely deferred assurance? And, above all, what kind of democracy are we building if the state responds to citizens demanding answers by making it increasingly difficult for them to be heard? The barricades around Jantar Mantar may eventually come down. Internet services may resume, trains may return to their schedules and security personnel may leave the streets. It can be diminished when political power becomes increasingly centralised, when dissent is treated as disruption and when a population is asked to accept decisions about its future without adequate space to challenge them. A government that believes in the strength of its democratic mandate should not fear questions from its citizens. And a country that believes in constitutional democracy must be willing to confront an uncomfortable truth: the freedoms it protects in its capital cannot be separated from the freedoms it permits in its peripheries. In 2019, Kashmir was told to accept a new political reality. Today, as Delhi confronts the possibility of extraordinary restrictions on protest, India must ask itself whether it is prepared to defend the democratic principles that Kashmiris insisted were never theirs alone. stories.headline: Historic Shah Kul: HC seeks updated report on demarcation, removal of encroachments
stories.title: Historic Shah Kul: HC seeks updated report on demarcation, removal of encroachments
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 14: The High Court of J&K and Ladakh has granted the authorities 10 more days to complete the ongoing demarcation and removal of encroachments from the Shah Kul -- a historical canal of importance and a national monument that had been the main source of water to Nishat Gardens since the time of Mughal Emperor Jahangir. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajesh Sekhri directed the authorities to submit a report updating the status of demarcation and removal of encroachments on the Shah Kul by October 27. The Court was hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by Mir Muhammad Shafi in 2023, seeking restoration of the centuries-old canal and removal of encroachments from its original alignment. During the proceeding, the court’s attention was drawn to the divisional commissioner Kashmir’s status report indicating constitution of a committee comprising the Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar; Vice Chairman, Lakes Conservation and Management Authority (LCMA); Regional Director, Survey and Land Records (Central), Srinagar; and Superintending Engineer, Irrigation and Flood Control, Srinagar. The committee formed pursuant to the September 15 order, has been tasked with consolidating the list of encroachments after proper demarcation with reference to revenue records, examining claims regarding property rights and preparing a time-bound action plan for removal of identified encroachments and restoration of Shah Kul. The Court was informed that the demarcation exercise had commenced and that voluntary removal as well as time-bound removal of encroachments was being undertaken simultaneously. It was also told that around 47 structures broadly fell within the scope of encroachment. Of these, 28 structures have so far been demarcated, while around 20 have already been removed. The remaining eight demarcated structures are likely to be removed shortly, they informed the court. Furthermore, the authorities further submitted that once the demarcation exercise is completed, any encroachers who fail to remove the structures voluntarily would face removal during an anti-encroachment drive. Allowing the 10-day time sought by them, the Bench directed the authorities to update the Court on the progress made in the demarcation and removal exercise.

stories.headline: Khadi and Village Industries: Weaving the Fabric of Inclusive and Sustainable India
stories.title: Khadi and Village Industries: Weaving the Fabric of Inclusive and Sustainable India
stories.summary: We are proud citizens of India -today the sixth largest economy in the world in terms of nominal GDP. Much of the economic growth is driven by the MSME sector contributing one-third in the overall GDP of the country. Herein again, major share comes from rural micro enterprises. The rural economy mainly relies on cottage industries like Khadi and handloom sector along with handicraft products manufactured from rural artisans. At a time when the world is grappling with inequality, climate change and resource depletion while in the domain of IT and software, AI is on relentless march gobbling up jobs, Khadi and Village Industries (KVI) can play an important role in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and strengthening the vision of an Atmanirbhar Bharat by enabling employment at differential skill levels, with low resource use locally mitigating migration too. Khadi, Hand spun and Hand woven, has been the Soul of Bharat. The responsible production is resource efficient on energy, water utilising natural fibres. The potential to be the driver of growth is being recognised steadily, albeit, slowly. Our industry signifies a rich cultural legacy from ancient times, exhibiting a diverse artistic sense with exemplary skill and personal touch of human emotions. Various written treatise pertaining to the Rigveda, Ramayana, Mahabharata, Thalia (by Greek historian Herodotus) and Kautilya have mentioned not only spinning and weaving but also the high quality of silk and cotton. While cotton has been cited in Ramayana and aligned to characteristics of Saint, the spectrum of weaves reflect the rich cultural tapestry. Through Khadi ‘Production by Masses’ using hand spun and hand woven, was utilised by Mahatma Gandhiji to confront Mass production by the Colonialists. The fabric of freedom is becoming aspirational fashion statement today because of its unique characteristics of being natural, comfortable and sustainable. Its handmade character gives it an individuality and hence it does not need to compete with generic production in volumes. The journey of Khadi—from a symbol of swadeshi and freedom to a contemporary fashion and lifestyle choice especially for environmentally aware new generation —demonstrates how tradition can adapt to changing consumer preferences. In fact, Tradition of near source production, which is more sustainable, is by default, intrinsic strength in Khadi ecosystem. In 21st Century, KVIC takes inspiration in our mandate from the clarion call of Hon’ble Prime Minister, “Khadi for Nation, Khadi for Fashion and Khadi for Transformation” while contributing to farm, fibre and market connect. It has to be noted that Hand spinning is the cardinal differentiator between Khadi and Handlooms. Since Yarn is also done by hand, the labour-intensive nature production enables employment to large section of people. The Khadi institutions, the aggregators of the hand-made hank produced in distributed architecture, have been assisted by Khadi and Village industries over last seven decades. Capacity enhancement through Skilling and up-skilling is being done through KVIC’s departmental and non-departmental training centers. With two-third of the rural population in the country, this sector holds larger significance as it provides ample opportunities for rural entrepreneurs. Such interventions directly advance SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by creating income-generating opportunities for people at the grassroots. Recent measures, including increases in spinning and weaving wages from April 2025 by Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), incremental support to improving working tools, conditions, tools infra, marketing interfaces, further demonstrate the emphasis on improving artisan incomes and making traditional livelihoods attractive and economically sustainable. The aggregate production has reached ~Rs 4000 crore(approx.) with Sales reaching about Rs 8000 crore(approx.) due to constant strengthening of the Khadi and Village industries (VI) Ecosystems over period, especially last one decade. Marching forward, the comfort fabric has been evolving into new categories and aspirational statements. Its transformation is evident in the emergence of Khadi denim, designer saris and bridal wear, contemporary shirts and trousers, and collections by mainstream brands such as Raymond and Peter England. Centre of Excellence for Khadi (NIFT, Delhi), an initiative between Ministry of MSME and Textiles, has developed 2129 Khadi design collections in the multiple categories of apparels, collections of home-made-ups, featuring prints, weaves, embroidery, and painting, sari designs and continues to enable the Khadi Institutions/ aspirants through CoEK knowledge portal. Our foray into infant wear is inspired by the fact that global infant and baby wear segment is expected to be exceeding $60 billion by 2030 (CAGR between 5-8.1%) and there would be priority to organic cotton, hypoallergenic fabrics and non-toxic manufacturing processes. Navyug Khadi designs reflecting positioning of Brand for 21st Century India, launched at National Crafts Museum & Hastkala Academy, Pragati Maidan with 710 new products presenting the “New Khadi of New India” in a contemporary and innovative manner along with Khadi Knowledge Portal. A collection of Wellness/Yoga wear ‘Svadha’ has been recently launched on International Yoga Day to attract all age groups from Gen Z to young at heart. Employment generation in Khadi requires very low investment. The assistance is being provided through schemes viz. Khadi Vikas Yojana, Gramodyog Vikas Yojana, PMEGP enabling KVI institutions/units in providing employment opportunities. The government is giving a major push to revive traditional industries by providing them all the necessary support including financial assistance, working capital facilitation, quality raw material support training, tool-kits, wage compensation, marketing support, promotion of digital payments and social security benefits. As per the evaluation study conducted by EDII, Ahmedabad, in its report submitted in January, 2026, over 75% of artisans across all the schemes reported a measurable increase in income post-intervention and a stable year-round employment was created for artisans who previously depended on seasonal or migratory labour which actually helped in reducing the migration of labour. Artisans trained under food processing, agarbatti, and Honey Mission have diversified into new product categories—such as essential oils, scented candles, or value-added honey derivatives. This diversification has improved resilience against local market fluctuations. Khadi directly addresses women’s empowerment and hence aligns to Inclusive development. Around 80 percent of around half a million Khadi artisans are women. Female participation was found to be dominating in GVY schemes, particularly in Agarbatti, Handmade Paper, Honey Mission, and Service Industry segments according to the study. Therefore, the engagement of a large number of women in any capacity in this sector has ensured direct remunerations for them, thus empowering them through financial independence and improved self-worth both within and outside of their homes. By enabling women to participate in productive economic activity, Khadi contributes directly to SDG 5 (Gender Equality) while also helping reduce social and economic disparities under SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities). The handmade industry has a growing global demand and huge export potential which needs to be tapped. With its quantum and varieties of traditional handmade products, India occupies an inevitable place in the world. 85% of the global handloom production occurs here and the ‘intrinsic value’ can be leveraged for ‘higher returns’. Other handloom nations like Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia manufacture very limited range of products but these are mainly for domestic production. India has the huge potential to cater to the global demand of Khadi and handloom products based on its demographic advantage and diversified cultural heritage. Consumers around the world are showing growing interest in products that are handmade, traceable, natural and environmentally responsible. This presents an opportunity to reposition Khadi and handmade products not merely as traditional goods, but as premium products that embody authenticity, strong backstory of craftsmanship and sustainability. KVIC has got registered as EPC on the Trade portal of Consulate General of India at New York, USA under Ministry of External Affairs. KVIC has initiated registering the progressive KIs with EXIM licenses and also engaging with Consulates in India for exposures to our strengths, which should enable building bridges. While Khadi has its recognition, the Brand is being protected through registering trade Mark in other countries so that our producers and value chains are protected. Further unique Branding, Geographical Identification (GI) tag has been recently awarded to Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) in respect of Ponduru Khadi which will enhance its value realisation for products of unique cotton and products spun and woven through equally unique process. The inaugural BRICS MSME Forum held in Agra this year exhibited specialized and premium products, including GI-tagged Ponduru Khadi, Bharat Kasturi Cotton, Bengal Muslin and naturally coloured cotton products. We need to ensure Quality and assurance in our products for enhancing new gen Z customer acquisition, retention and higher value returns for such niche products . Towards this end, the department's Central Sliver Plant (CSP), established nearly three and a half decades ago, are being modernized. Of the five currently operational CSPs, the plants located in Chittaradurga, Karnataka, and Kuttur, Kerala, have completed modernization and are operational. The Sliver plant in Karnataka utilises Solar energy for 50% of the requirement while wind power is being explored to make the production totally environmentally supportive. This approach resonates with SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) by connecting traditional enterprises with design, technology, modern markets and evolving supply chains. Technology Up-gradation of Khadi Institutions’ Production Infrastructure and technology-based Common Facility Centres (CFCs) are proposed to strengthen Village Industries clusters through shared infrastructure and modern processing facilities. KVIC is enabling Traceability solutions across the value chains which should enable integrating IT to tradition and attract new gen interest in the production ecosystem also. Last but not the least, the cottage industry is eco-friendly in nature being energy efficient, water efficient and use of natural fibres/ colours . Khadi is an eco- friendly fabric with very less carbon footprint and environmentally sustainable. The measurement of this is being studied by premier Institutions (IIT, IIMs) to enable suitably factoring in the product as well as Brand promotion narrative to agile new gen consumer – domestic and international. article_sentences: The Supreme Court will hear today the petitions concerning the Delhi protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, including pleas alleging police excesses against protesters, journalists and lawyers, contempt case over restrictions on public transport, and a challenge to the constitutional validity of a provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).

The petition by Rahul Gandhi challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the petitions concerning the gathering and alleged disruption at the Supreme Court premises on October 12, when Rahul Gandhi and other Opposition leaders marched towards the Court Registry to file a petition challenging the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise are also listed.
The matters are listed before Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi at 10:30 am.

The cases include petitions filed by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders, CPI(M) General Secretary MA Baby, RJD MP Manoj Jha, former MP Digvijaya Singh, senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP Menaka Guruswamy, AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi, the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA), journalists' organisations and individual petitioners.
Petitions were initially filed challenging restrictions imposed by the Union and Delhi authorities ahead of the October 10 protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party and others.

Subsequent petitions have raised allegations of non-compliance with the Supreme Court's directions, illegal detention of protesters and lawyers, assault and harassment of journalists covering the demonstrations, and restrictions on movement and communication.
The October 9 order addressed restrictions imposed on Metro stations and train services in anticipation of the demonstrations.
The Court directed authorities to regulate transport rather than impose a blanket prohibition, while ensuring that the arrangements did not unnecessarily impede the public's movement.
Advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi filed a contempt petition alleging that authorities continued to restrict Metro and train services despite the October 9 directions.

The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) and the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA) have approached the Court over alleged detention and manhandling of advocates during the protests.
The SCBA has sought details of detained advocates and the police personnel involved.

It has also sought disclosure of prohibitory orders and preservation of relevant records, along with safeguards to ensure that lawyers can access courts and discharge their professional responsibilities.

article_sentences: The Delhi government has approved a new industrial policy that outlines a ten-year roadmap for developing a clean, knowledge-based industrial economy in the Capital, with a focus on high-value, non-polluting sectors, according to a statement from the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) said on Wednesday.

The Industrial Policy, 2026, approved in a Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, also allocated Rs 1,000 crore under Mukhyamantri Udyamshree Yojana for five years to promote new industries and create jobs, said the statement.

Under the new policy, special incentives will be given for 10 priority sectors, including Information Technology (IT), global capability centres, data centres, healthcare, research and modern manufacturing, as per the CMO.
“Women-led micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) will receive additional support for business modernisation and expansion.
Employers hiring women will receive higher incentives for each woman recruited.
Women and young people will also receive special attention under skill development programmes.
These provisions aim to expand business and employment opportunities for women entrepreneurs and employees,” said the statement.
Ms. Gupta said the policy focuses on making better use of the Capital’s economic potential by encouraging advanced technology, research, specialised services and high-value-added industries.

“Over the next 10 years, it aims to create an investment-friendly environment, provide necessary support to entrepreneurs, promote women-led enterprises and generate new employment opportunities for young people.
It will also seek to steer Delhi’s industrial economy towards a more modern, cleaner and knowledge-based model,” she said.

Ms. Gupta said that considering the needs of different sectors, tailored incentives would be provided for capital investment, office or workspace rentals, new hiring, research, certification, technological modernisation, energy conservation and skill development.
The policy will also encourage resource reuse and waste reduction, she added.

stories.headline: Medical fraternity must bridge urban-rural healthcare gaps: LG Sinha
stories.title: Medical fraternity must bridge urban-rural healthcare gaps: LG Sinha
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 14: Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Wednesday urged the medical fraternity to bridge the urban-rural healthcare gaps. Congratulating Government Medical College (GMC), Srinagar, for organising a conference on 'Advancing Internal Medicine: From Evidence to Excellence in Clinical Practice', LG Sinha said, “Medical science is making historic advances, and new drugs and diagnostic tools have opened up new possibilities for treatment. The greatest need today is to ensure that these innovations are not available only to physicians in large cities, but also reach doctors in villages. We must ensure that there is not even the slightest gap between urban and rural areas in access to facilities and available tools. This should be the first objective of this conference.” He underscored the critical role of internal medicine in delivering holistic and patient-centric healthcare. The LG said that physicians often face the challenging task of identifying complex underlying health conditions from seemingly simple symptoms. He said that the strength of internal medicine lies in its ability to view the human body as an interconnected system and to understand the complete medical story of a patient through clinical knowledge, experience and careful observation. LG Sinha said that observation, reason, human understanding, and courage remain the defining qualities of a physician. He said that physicians frequently serve as the first point of medical contact for families and, in many cases, build enduring relationships across generations, rooted in trust, compassion, and scientific evidence. The LG lauded GMC Srinagar for its significant contribution to medical education and healthcare, noting that generations of doctors trained by the institution continue to serve across Jammu Kashmir and the country. He also highlighted the emerging healthcare challenges. “While infectious diseases remain a concern, lifestyle-related disorders such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, fatty liver disease and cardiovascular ailments are assuming epidemic proportions. We need to ensure that advances in diagnostics, therapeutics and medical technologies reach physicians and patients in rural and remote areas as effectively as they do in urban centres,” LG Sinha said. He also called upon the medical fraternity to strengthen indigenous research and generate evidence relevant to India’s diverse population. The LG said that the country’s demographic diversity, combined with the expertise and commitment of doctors, presents immense opportunities for scientific discovery and innovation. He also outlined a five-year roadmap and proposed six key commitments for the medical community including expanding access to advanced medical knowledge through digital health platforms and telemedicine, prioritising preventive healthcare and early detection of diseases, using technology and artificial intelligence as supportive tools while preserving clinical judgement, continuously strengthening research capacity, ensuring the wellbeing of doctors and addressing professional burnout and preserving human compassion at the centre of healthcare delivery. LG Sinha urged the young doctors to remain curious, embrace innovation and learn from experienced mentors. He called upon senior physicians to generously share their clinical wisdom and guide the next generation of healthcare professionals. “Early detection of diabetes, hypertension and liver disease is less costly and can help reduce treatment expenses. I urge all physicians and internists to lead prevention campaigns at the community level, because a doctor’s voice can have an extraordinary influence on society. I have every confidence that people will take your advice seriously when it comes to preventing lifestyle-related diseases," the LG said. "We must value physicians’ hard work, service and dedication. Along with caring for patients, hospitals and institutions, it should be ensured that doctors are cared for too. Providing them with better workplaces and working conditions should be a priority.”

stories.summary: Prescript: The World Bank which developed the concept of the Ease of Doing Business in 2003 officially discontinued it in 2021 because of major data manipulations. During 2024-2026, the Bank rolled out a redesigned framework, Business Ready (B-READY) which shifts the focus from narrow regulatory checkboxes to evaluating a country’s business environment, balancing the ease of commercial operations with public interest protections like environmental sustainability and labour rights. Historically placed in the lowest tier of “Emerging Business Ecosystems” in India, J&K climbed rather dramatically to 5th rank in the Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) in 2025. There is no local-founder preference, no differential land term, no reserved park plots, and no scoring of proposals by local ownership. The preference for locals in employment that the EoDB has is enabling rather than operative. The Executive Committee may order that every enterprise with more than 10 employees to reserve a percentage of vacancies for domicile candidates. But without fixing any percentage in the Bill. Worse still, units with 10 or fewer workers which is the bulk of J&K establishments are outside even this power. Better to keep the employment-reservation power but make the percentage and the exemption process statutory and uniform and exempt local enterprises below a turnover threshold. The idea and intent have to be to give local enterprises concrete process benefits. Local enterprises being ones with majority ownership or control is by domicile individuals, cooperatives or producer companies. For example, priority in the 7- or 10-day tracks when capacity or plots are limited, or a longer inspection moratorium; four years instead of three. There has to be policy signalling. In addition to ownership, the EoDB simplifications should be stratified by size. Kashmir industry is overwhelmingly micro; it contributes 60 percent of industrial investment and close to 90 percent of industrial employment. The Bill must have size tools. This could include introducing a turnover band, a micro-versus-medium fee, no working-capital or inspection rule scaled to a 2-to-10-person workshop. Third, a lighter path should be created for a household enterprise as against a park-based plants. The fast lane in the EoDB Act is location: an approved industrial park gets three days; a unit outside waits ten times more! In a place where most units are not in parks, the size structure of the business and the speed structure of the Bill point in different directions. Fourth, a big fillip could have been given to logistics, which doesn’t even find a mention in the bill. The District Empowered Committee, for instance, could be empowered to have an “access protocol”; priority movement windows, coordination with security forces, traffic and disaster authorities. This will ensure export goods movement (and closures) are managed by rule rather than ad-hoc orders of security forces. The instances of apples rotting on the road because of security forces’ movement are too many to recount. Finally, environment in the EoDB is a retained constraint, not an incentive. That is deregulation of process, not a green preference. To go green has to be incentivised by fast tracking operational permissions, provide renewable-energy setoffs, give longer moratorium for effluent or energy standards and emissions. These clauses remain inside a process statute: they accelerate and structurally favour the home-grown businesses and land-efficient projects that the local economy needs. Postscript: Domain experts have red flagged the EoDB Act enabling executive relaxations to bypass statutory Master Plans which risk environmental vulnerability. Valid as these concerns may be, they demand serious introspection, not shooting the messenger as has been done by the industry bodies. Despite elaborate master plans, beginning with the Srinagar Master Plan 1971–91 nearly fifty years ago, the city has seen only haphazard growth, illegal colonies, encroachments on government land, and development in flood-prone or ecologically sensitive areas. What gives? Their practical contribution has been marginal because of implementation and enforcement shortfalls. The contention is not to support wanton development but to introspect how master plans should be redone as living, enforceable frameworks that protect Kashmir’s fragile ecology and mitigate disaster risks. Rigid paper blueprints, as the Master plans have been, are meant to be bypassed. The author is a Contributing Editor of Greater Kashmir.

stories.headline: The Himalayas Cannot Be Developed Into Submission
stories.title: The Himalayas Cannot Be Developed Into Submission
stories.summary: The Lieutenant Governor’s call for a comprehensive, science-based and people-centric approach to mountain development comes at a time when the Himalayan region can no longer afford the luxury of delay. Across Jammu and Kashmir, the signs of ecological stress are visible in shrinking water sources, unstable slopes, erratic weather, forest degradation, unplanned construction and the growing vulnerability of settlements to disasters. The crisis is no longer theoretical. It is increasingly shaping the lives and livelihoods of mountain communities. The message delivered at the Sustainable Mountain Development Summit correctly places the Himalayas at the centre of India’s environmental and developmental concerns. These mountains are not merely scenic landscapes or tourism destinations. They are the source of rivers, reservoirs of biodiversity and natural regulators of climate. Any disturbance to their ecological balance carries consequences far beyond the immediate location of the damage. Yet, the central challenge lies in translating a sound vision into enforceable action. For decades, development in the mountains has often been pursued through a plains-based model—wider roads, larger buildings, expanding towns and rising tourist numbers—with insufficient regard for the region’s fragile carrying capacity. Roads are carved into unstable slopes, construction continues along water channels and flood-prone areas, and waste accumulates in places that lack the infrastructure to manage it. Such development may produce short-term economic gains, but it deepens long-term public risk. The proposed emphasis on science-based carrying capacity and zoning is therefore fundamental. No town, valley or tourist destination should be permitted to grow beyond what its water, land, drainage, waste-management and emergency systems can sustain. Carrying-capacity assessments must not remain policy language confined to summit documents. They must determine where construction is allowed, what kind of infrastructure is suitable and how many visitors a destination can safely accommodate. Climate-resilient infrastructure is equally urgent. Mountain roads, bridges, buildings and public facilities must be designed for local terrain and changing weather patterns. Modern technology can improve forecasting and early-warning systems, but it must work alongside the knowledge of communities that have lived with the mountains for generations. Local experience can often identify the first signs of a landslide, flood or water crisis long before formal systems respond. The focus on regenerative livelihoods offers another important direction. High-value horticulture, organic farming, sericulture, eco-tourism and other green enterprises can reduce pressure on fragile ecosystems while creating opportunities for youth and women. But this requires access to markets, credit, training and reliable infrastructure. Empowerment cannot be reduced to slogans; it must be supported by sustained institutional investment. The proposed zero-waste and circular mountain economy must also become a public priority. Tourist destinations and urban centres cannot continue generating waste without adequate systems for segregation, recycling, sewage treatment and scientific disposal. The Himalayas do not need development at any cost. They need development that understands limits. Tradition and technology, economic ambition and ecological restraint must move together. The true measure of a developed region will not be the height of its buildings or the number of tourists it attracts, but whether its rivers flow, its slopes remain stable, and its people can live securely within the limits of nature.
